items.title: Harry Allen interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997
items.q: through listening to Scott I began to be aware of ... Zoot now

ctx.x: Maybe you didn’t go to class that year. Did your tastes in music work backwards. After working in your head with Scott, did you go back farther than that?

Not really my taste so much as my awareness of where Scott came from and through listening to Scott I began to be aware of Ben Webster and Lester Young and Coleman Hawkins and Paul Gonsalves and Zoot now and Stan Getz. And so I went backwards in that sense — not so much a taste sense but just an awareness.

items.title: Harry Allen interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997
items.q: it’s not just like Zoot Sims played all of them but he didn’t know them technically, he couldn’t write them down for you. He just heard them.

ctx.x: What about yourself? This is a hard question and I don’t always ask it, but when you’re improvising, what are you thinking about?

Well as Stan Getz used to say that what he was thinking about was trying to psych himself into being relaxed. So I think about being relaxed. And it’s sort of combination — technically, because of my training I technically know the chords that we’re playing and it’s not just like Zoot Sims played all of them but he didn’t know them technically, he couldn’t write them down for you. He just heard them. Well with me it’s a combination because I know what they are, but I also hear them and it’s sort of a combination…

When you are in a situation like today when you have four tenor saxes, do you go out of your way to either play off what someone else is doing — try to play different from what someone else is doing, or do you just let it rip?
